title: Acute limb ischaemia
subtitle: Heparin now, classify, revascularise by the clock

sources.title: ESVS 2020 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Acute Limb Ischaemia

sources.org: Fogarty TJ et al., Surgery, Gynecology and Obstetrics
sources.title: A method for extraction of arterial emboli and thrombi

red_flags.text: Sensory loss beyond the toes, or any muscle weakness. The limb is immediately threatened (Rutherford IIb) and needs revascularisation without delay.
Rigid, tender calf muscles, fixed mottling that does not blanch, and paralysis. These suggest irreversible ischaemia (Rutherford III).
Bilateral leg ischaemia, or ischaemia with abdominal pain: think saddle embolus, aortic dissection or concurrent mesenteric embolus.
A cold leg with a palpable popliteal pulse on the other side, or a pulsatile popliteal fossa: thrombosed popliteal aneurysm, which has a high amputation rate.
Rising potassium, acidosis, dark urine or a swollen tense leg after revascularisation: reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome.

do_now.text: Give an intravenous bolus of unfractionated heparin as soon as acute limb ischaemia is diagnosed, unless there is a contraindication.
Call the vascular surgeon immediately. A threatened limb has hours, not a day.
Classify the limb now using the Rutherford acute categories: I viable, IIa marginally threatened, IIb immediately threatened, III irreversible. The class sets the clock.
Analgesia, keep the limb dependent and protected, avoid heat and pressure on the heel.

assess.text: The six Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold. Sensory and motor function are what separate IIa from IIb.
Test sensation in the foot and dorsiflexion of the toes. Loss of light touch and weakness of the toes are early; calf tenderness is late.

Embolus or thrombosis: sudden onset, a known source such as AF, normal pulses in the other leg favour embolus. Claudication history and absent contralateral pulses favour thrombosis on existing disease.
Handheld Doppler at the ankle: an inaudible arterial signal with an audible venous signal fits class II, and the neurology decides IIa from IIb. Loss of the venous signal as well suggests class III.
Check the other leg, both arms and the abdomen. Emboli rarely travel alone.

investigate.text: ECG, FBC, U&E, CK, coagulation, group and save. Baseline potassium and CK before reperfusion.
CT angiography for IIa, and for IIb only if it will not delay revascularisation. IIb with a clear embolic history can go straight to theatre with on-table angiography.
Duplex ultrasound for a suspected popliteal aneurysm, of both popliteal fossae.
Echocardiography after the limb is safe, to look for a cardiac source of embolus.

resuscitate.text: Continue heparin infusion before and after revascularisation per local protocol, then plan long-term anticoagulation for an embolic source.
Correct hypovolaemia and monitor urine output: reperfusion releases potassium, acid and myoglobin.
Measure potassium and CK in the hours after reperfusion and treat hyperkalaemia promptly.

definitive.text: IIb: immediate revascularisation. IIa: urgent revascularisation, with time for imaging and planning.
Embolus: surgical balloon catheter embolectomy, usually from the groin, with completion imaging. The technique has changed little since its description.

Thrombosis on existing disease: catheter-directed thrombolysis, percutaneous thrombectomy, or bypass, chosen on anatomy and the time the limb can tolerate. Thrombolysis is slower and is best kept for limbs that can wait.
Consider four-compartment fasciotomy after revascularisation of a limb with prolonged or severe ischaemia, and perform it through two incisions.
Rutherford III: primary amputation or palliation. Revascularising a dead limb risks fatal reperfusion injury.

escalate.text: Consultant vascular surgeon for every IIb and III limb, and for any decision for amputation or palliation.
If there is no vascular service, transfer immediately after heparin. Do not wait for CT in the referring hospital if it will delay transfer.
Interventional radiology for thrombolysis or hybrid procedures; cardiology for the embolic source.
Critical care for reperfusion injury, hyperkalaemia or renal failure.

notes: The question is not 'is there a pulse' but 'can the patient feel and move the toes'. Neurology is the clock.
Embolus and thrombosis look alike in the first hour and behave very differently on the table. A failed embolectomy in a diseased artery is a thrombosis and needs a different operation.
Fasciotomy done early is a scar; fasciotomy done late is a debridement. If you are wondering, do it.
